drills.coachNote: Look at this — your king's only real shield on the a2-g8 diagonal was the pawn on g7, and g6 opens the door. The moment you play it, White has Qc4+, hitting your king along that diagonal and forcing Kh7, then g4 kicks your queen off h5 back to e5, and a position you were winning by nearly three pawns is suddenly level. Qb5 was the move — active, eyeing the b4 pawn, and it leaves your king's cover alone. In queen endings, don't move a shield pawn just because nothing's attacking it yet — ask what diagonal it's covering first.

drills.coachNote: Your knight jumping to e4 lands on the same diagonal as f5 — which is also the diagonal your king on h7 sits on. White plays Qf5+, and that single move does two jobs: checks your king, forcing Kh8, then Qxe4 just scoops the knight for free since nothing else was covering it. That's how you go from a pawn and a half up to down a whole piece in two moves. Qe8 was right instead — it keeps your queen active without handing the knight a square where one check wins it. Before parking a piece somewhere, check what other line or diagonal already touches that square.

drills.coachNote: Nothing new was threatening you, but the b4 pawn was already hanging — your king move to f3 doesn't defend it and doesn't do anything else useful either. Black takes Rxb4, and now you have to walk the king back to e2 anyway, so you've burned a tempo for nothing while black's rook swings to a4 and then breaks with e6-e4, ripping the center open. Nf3 was the move that mattered — it heads for d4, a fantastic central outpost, and even though b4 still falls in that line, you get real compensation through active piece play. When a pawn's already lost, spend the move improving your worst piece, not shuffling the king.

drills.coachNote: Your rook on c2 was the only thing guarding the c3 pawn, and Rd2 walks it off that job for no reason — black just plays Rxc3 and the pawn's gone. Then Ne4 and Ra3 hand black's rook real activity while you're down material with nothing to show for it. Kd3 does a similar job in terms of activating a piece, but it keeps defending c3 while bringing your king into the game, and even after ...Bxa6 you get to swing your rook to a2 and win the a7 pawn right back. Before rerouting a piece, check whether it's the only thing guarding something.

drills.coachNote: Your king on g6 is already living dangerously, and the real problem is the bishop on c4 aiming at f7 with the knight on g5 backing it up — Rh8 ignores that completely. White plays Bxf7#, mate, because your king has no escape once that diagonal opens with check. You were up over three pawns and none of it mattered since the mating net around your own king went unanswered. Nh5 was the move — it hits the queen on h4 with tempo, forcing Qxg5 and a trade-down instead of a mate. When your king's this exposed, ask first whether a move stops you getting mated, not whether it looks useful.

drills.coachNote: Bg4 attacks the queen on f3, but she just steps to g3 — and from there she's still eyeing g7 next to your own king, with the knight on h3 ready to join the attack. You haven't gained anything, you've just spent a move helping White relocate the queen to a better square. Nc6 was the natural move instead — it develops your last minor piece and sets up ...Nh5, which actually hits the queen with a real threat and forces her somewhere worse. Only chase the queen when she has nowhere good to go; otherwise you're just improving her position for free.

Rh1 does nothing about it; it just steps aside while black plays Qxf2#, mate, because your own pieces box the king in with no flight square. You were already down over four pawns, but this made it terminal. Rxg3 was the fix — grabbing that pawn directly removes the defender of f2 and kills the mating idea, even if you're still fighting uphill afterward. When a pawn is propping up a mating pattern, capture it before anything else.

drills.coachNote: Both Rg1 and Rh2 attack the queen on g2, but only one of them keeps guarding h3 at the same time, and that's the whole difference. Play Rg1 and the rook leaves the h-file, so black plays Qxh3 and the queen escapes clean because nothing's left to recapture. Rh2 attacks the queen along rank two while still covering h3 down the file, so she has nowhere safe to go — Qxh2, Nxh2 just wins your rook back and more, netting a full queen for a knight. When you're trying to trap a piece, make sure every escape square stays covered before you move the piece that was covering it.

drills.coachNote: You're already up a piece, so trading is the last thing you want. Qg5+ is check, which feels tempting, but Black just answers Qxg5, and after Nxg5 the queens are off - then Ne5 jumps in and claws back activity you didn't need to give. Qf4 keeps queens on where your material edge counts: Black plays Qd6, you repeat Qg5+ forcing Qf6 away, then Qxd5 grabs the pawn clean with nothing but Rd8 in response. When you're already winning material, don't chase checks that trade pieces - keep the tension and let your extra piece do the work.

drills.title: vs Mohamed_Behery (840) — Queens Pawn Opening Horwitz Defense
drills.coachNote: Nxh7 grabs a pawn, but your knight on f6 had a much scarier jump. Nd5+ is check on e7 and simultaneously forks the queen on c7 - Black's only way out is exd5, handing back the knight to save the queen. Compare that to what actually happened: after Nxh7, Black plays Rd8, and following Qf6+ Ke8 the king simply escapes to safety and your attack fizzles. With Nd5+, after exd5 you continue Rfe1+, driving the king to d6, then Qxf8+ wins the rook outright with check. Whenever a knight move gives check AND hits a second piece, that's the move to look for first.

drills.title: vs edekyihotmailcom (766) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: This one stings - you had forced mate in two. Nf4+ pushes the king to e3, its only legal square since your own pieces cover everything else, and Bc5 is then checkmate, with the bishop on d5 sealing e3 shut. Instead Qxe5+ grabs a pawn with check, but White blocks with Ne4, and after Bxe4, Qc1 and O-O-O let the king slip away to safety on the queenside. You dropped from a forced mate down to just a big material edge. Whenever the enemy king is stuck in the center, scan every check for a mating net before reaching for the free pawn.

Ne6 instead just repositions your knight and lets White untangle with Qc1, easing the pressure. Notice when a king has no safe squares to run to - that's when you keep checking rather than pausing to develop.

drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Look at the diagonal from d1 to g4 — e2 and f3 are both empty, so White's queen on d1 is staring straight down it. The moment your knight jumps from e5 to g4, it lands right on that diagonal undefended, and Qxg4 just wins the piece for free — after e5, Qg3, Re8 you're down a full knight for nothing, which is your whole four-and-a-half-pawn swing. c5 was the move: it grabs space and preps ...Nc6, and after Re1 Nc6 b4 b6 Bb2 you're developing calmly without putting a piece on a square the enemy queen already owns. Before jumping a knight forward, check every line the enemy queen currently controls.

drills.explanation: Bxa2 trades off White's light-squared bishop on your terms: after Rxa2 you swing rooks to the e-file with Rae8 and Re6, sitting solidly behind the e5 pawn. Rad8 left the bishops eyeballing each other one move too long — Bh6 came with threats at your king, and after g6, Bxe6 fxe6 left you with doubled, weak e-pawns.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on e6 and White's bishop on a2 sit on the same diagonal — nothing of yours covers a2, so your bishop is actually the one hanging. Bxa2 fixes that on your terms: you trade bishops, and after Rxa2 Rae8 Ra1 Re6 Bd2 you're simplifying into the winning position you already had. Rad8 ignored it instead, and White answered Bh6, g6, Bxe6, fxe6 — the a2 bishop simply reaches across and takes yours while your rook move did nothing about it, giving back a pawn and a half even though you stayed winning overall. When two bishops line up on the same diagonal, resolve that before you play anything else.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 wins a full rook: the knight captures its counterpart and forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so after Qd6 saves the queen, Nxd8 collects the rook and Qxg5 even adds a pawn. a4 instead gave Black time for Nxe5, trading off your monster knight, and after Qxe5 his other knight landed on e4 with real counterplay.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your knight on e5 is one hop from a fork — landing on c6 it hits both the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, and nothing black has stops it. Nxc6 cashes in: even with Qd6 instead of a recapture, Nxd8 Qxd8 Qxg5 Rg8 shows you winning the exchange plus a pawn, matching how winning you already were. Instead a4 ignored the fork completely, giving Black time to play Nxe5 himself — trading off the very knight that was about to fork him — and after Qxe5 Ne4 f3 the tactic is simply gone, costing four and a half pawns. When a knight is one move from forking a queen and a rook, play that move first.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 is a fork: from c6 the knight hits both the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so bxc6 is forced — wrecking the pawn cover in front of the king on c8. Then Qd3 turns on the knight on e4, and after Nxc5 bxc5 you're clearly on top. b5 abandoned the b4 pawn's guard of your c5 knight, and Nxe5 won material — no recapture worked.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: The same shot from last move is still on the board — Ne5-c6 still forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8. This time Black recaptures normally: Nxc6 bxc6 Qd3 Nxc5 bxc5 a5 trades down cleanly while also removing his annoying knight on e4. You pushed b5 instead, ignoring the fork a second time, and now Black gets there first with Nxe5 — after bxa6 bxa6 Nb3 you've traded pieces without ever cashing in on the tactic, and the initiative swings to Black, another four and a half pawns gone. A tactic doesn't expire because you missed it once — if Nxc6 was right last move, check whether it's still right before reaching for a pawn push again.

drills.explanation: Rxf7 forces mate in three: your queen on d5 X-rays g8 so f7 can't really be held, and after Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate — the bishop on f6 seals g7 while the queen on d5 guards g8, so the rook can't be taken. Qg5 instead let Black play Rxf2 and keep the counterplay alive.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: You had a forced mate on the board. Rxf7 rips away his king's last pawn cover, and after Re2 Rg7+ Kh8 Rg8# your rook and the bishop on f6 seal every escape square — mate in three. Instead you played Qg5, a slower try that forces nothing, and it handed Black the tempo he needed: Rxf2 tears into your own king's shelter, and Qe5, Rf3, Rf1 shows his queen on b2, rook on c2, and passed d4 pawn crashing through on you instead — an eighteen-pawn swing that turned a completely winning position into a loss. When you're already crushing and there's a forcing line on the board, calculate that first; a slower move only makes sense once you've ruled out the mate.

drills.explanation: Qxc8 wins the rook on c8 outright — Black never dares recapture, since your bishop on f6 and rook on e7 strangle his king; he tries Qb5, and after Re8 he must throw his queen away with Qf1+ Rxf1. Qd5 let a won game slip: Qxa3, and after Qxd4, Qxh3 stripped your king — nearly fifteen pawns of advantage gone.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Take a breath here — before Qd5, look at your queen on c4 and Black's rook on c8: they're on the same file with nothing in between, so Qxc8 just wins the rook outright, no strings attached. Instead Qd5 hands the tempo to Black's queen on b2, and she goes to work — Qxa3, then Qxd4, then Qxh3, gobbling your pawns and cracking open your king while your rooks stand idle. You were up nearly nineteen pawns of advantage there; that swing of almost fifteen pawns is you handing back a completely won game. The lesson: before playing any 'nice' queen move, scan every open file and diagonal for a piece just sitting there — Qxc8 was the whole position.

drills.explanation: The g5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxg5 meets that head-on — the knight is covered by that same bishop, and after fxg5 Bxg5 Black's kingside pawns are stripped while his pieces retreat to passive squares like Nf6 and Nb8 as Qf3 builds pressure. Bf5+ dropped a whole piece instead: e6 blocked the check and hit the bishop, and after Bc2, gxf4 won your dark-squared bishop.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: This is the exact same picture as two moves ago — your bishop on f4 is still hanging to that pawn on g5, and you reached for Bf5+ again instead of fixing it. Nxg5 was sitting right there: it removes the attacker on g5 and wins a pawn, and after fxg5 Bxg5 you've blasted open the kingside pawns in front of Black's king, which is still stuck on d7 because he hasn't castled — Nf6 and Qf3 keep the pressure coming. Playing Bf5+ again just repeats the pattern: ...e6 shoves the bishop back to c2 and you're no closer to solving the g5 problem. When the same tension sits on the board for several moves, ask why it's still there before making another 'active-looking' move.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Look at your bishop on f4 — Black's pawn on g5 is staring right at it, so that bishop is hanging the moment you don't deal with it. Bf5+ feels active because it's check, but it completely ignores that threat: after ...e6 kicks your other bishop back to c2, Black simply plays gxf4 and just wins your bishop for free, then castles into safety with O-O. The engine's e4 accepts that trade differently — it blasts the center open first, so after gxf4 exd5 you're ripping into his position and Qa4+ picks up tempo and structure to compensate for the piece. The principle: when a piece is attacked, a flashy check elsewhere doesn't make the threat disappear.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight jumps to g5, but look at the bishop still sitting on c1 — it's aimed straight down that c1-g5 diagonal, so g5 is exactly the square it wants to land on. Bxg5 just wins the knight clean, and then f6, Nxe5 grabs your e5 pawn too since it's left undefended in the fallout, and Be6 mops up — you're down real material for nothing. Nd6 was the calm, correct idea: it tucks the knight onto a safe, central square that still supports your bishop on f5, and after Rxe5+ Be7 Qe2 Bg6 Bf4 the position stays balanced. Before jumping a piece forward, check what's already aiming at that square — here it was a bishop that hadn't even moved.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Same diagonal as before — the bishop on c1 is still eyeing g5, and your knight is still sitting there, so Be7 doesn't solve anything; it just develops while ignoring the piece that's actually hanging. White plays Bxg5, simply winning your knight, and even though Be6 and Bxe7 Qxe7 trade off a pair of bishops afterward, you're still down a full knight for the exchange. Ne6 was the move that actually addresses the problem: it pulls the knight off the attacked square and drops it onto a strong central post supporting f5, and the position stays roughly level after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 Qd5. When a piece is under fire, your first candidate move has to deal with that piece, not develop somewhere else.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Here your bishop on f4 has a great trick available — Bc7 jumps in and attacks the queen on d8 directly, since Black hasn't had time to move her or free up the bishop on c8 yet. That forces Qd7, and then b6 followed by Nc6 keeps squeezing the queenside where his pieces are still tangled up. Instead you played e4, a natural-looking central push, but it gives Black exactly the tempo he needed: he plays Bd7, finally freeing that bishop, and by the time you get to Bc7 later it's Qc8 defending calmly and b6 holding everything together — the moment's gone. The lesson is about timing: a good idea like Bc7 loses its punch if you let the opponent untangle first.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Qc5 was the move that kept the pressure on — it restricts Black's queen on b6 and sets up Bd6, which hits both the rook on f8 and the knight on e7 at once; after Qd8 Bd6 Re8, Bxe7 just wins that knight and Rxe7 is forced. Qc3 looks similar but doesn't actually threaten anything, so Black gets a free move to play Bd7, developing the bishop that had been stuck on c8. Once that happens the tables turn a little — Black even swings Bxb5 and grabs your pawn because nothing was watching it once your pieces weren't working toward the same target. When you have a move that creates a concrete threat, don't trade it for one that just looks natural.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were completely winning here, up more than four points of material, and your knight on d6 has a beautiful shot: Nf5+ forks the king on g3 and the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 Nxg7, you simply win the rook and the game is over — Ke5 Nh5 c4 and your pawns roll through. Instead Nb7 walks the knight to a square where it's just hanging with no support, and White answers Rc7+, forcing your king to d8, then Rxb7 scoops it up for free — a twelve-pawn swing that turns a winning endgame into a losing one. Whenever your knight can reach a square that hits the enemy king, always check first whether it's also hitting something bigger, like a rook.

drills.explanation: Bxg3+ wins a pawn with check, and after the forced Kxg3, Rxd1 scoops the rook — d1 had no defender at all, so you net rook and pawn for the bishop. Rd7 put your rook on a square nothing defends (the knight on c6 doesn't cover d7): Rxd7 took it for free, and after Bd6, bxc6 grabbed your knight as well.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were completely winning, up more than six pawns of evaluation, but Rd7 walks your rook straight onto the same open d-file as White's rook on d1 — nothing of yours controls d2 through d6, so Rxd7 just wins the rook for free and the whole game flips. Notice your bishop on f4 had a shot the entire time: Bxg3+ forks the king onto g3, and once Kxg3 happens the d-file is yours uncontested, so Rxd1 wins the rook clean instead. From there you're simply mopping up with Be3, Ne7, Bxa7 — a totally winning ending. Before parking a rook on an open file, always ask who else already owns it.

drills.explanation: Qxb7+ forces checkmate: the queen grabs b7 and checks the king on e7 along the wide-open seventh rank, Black must block with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate — your knight on f6 covers the escape squares e8 and d7, and the e5 pawn guards the knight. exd4 was a pawn grab with mate on the board; after Bg7 Black started breathing again.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black's king on e7 is stuck in the middle of the board, defended only by the queen on d8, and that's a huge weakness along the 7th rank that you walked past by playing exd4. Qxb7+ hits that exact rank — b7 through e7 is a clean line — so it's check, and the queen on d8 is the only piece that can block, forced to Qc7; then Qxc7# is mate because the king on e7 has no square to run to. Instead you just recaptured a pawn, letting Bg7 develop and the position drift back down from a forced mate to merely winning. When a king sits alone on an open rank, always scan that rank for a queen check first.

drills.explanation: Rd7+ is a deflection: the queen on c7 has to capture, and Nxd7 then forks the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 — you've won queen for rook, with Rd1 coming to support the knight. Nd7 tried the fork without the preparation: Bg7 simply stepped the bishop out, nothing was won, and Rd6 got met by Rbc8. The open d-file was the key — use it with check first.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your knight on f6 already eyes d7, and that's exactly why the rook sac works first: Rd7+ is check, and the only piece that can block is the queen on c7, so Qxd7 is forced — then Nxd7 recaptures and you've won the queen for a rook. By playing Nd7 directly you skipped the check that forces the queen onto that losing square, so Black just plays Bg7 and consolidates, shrinking your edge from 'win the queen' down to a normal advantage. The lesson: when a piece of yours already covers a square, look for a way to force the enemy queen onto it before you just occupy it yourself.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a4 was attacked by the knight on c5 and had to reach safety first — Qa3 does it. The Qh4 attacking idea was right but needed f6 first: after f6 gxf6, Black's own pawn on f6 blocks the e7–h4 diagonal, and only then is Qh4 strong. Played immediately, Qh4 landed right on the e7-queen's diagonal — Qxh4 won your queen on the spot.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black's queen on e7 sits on the e7-h4 diagonal, and Qh4 marches your own queen right onto it — Qxh4 wins your queen for nothing, and that swing turns a bad-but-fighting position into a lost one. You were already down about four and a half pawns of evaluation, so this wasn't the moment to get careless with the queen; it was the moment to tuck her somewhere safe. Qa3 does exactly that — off the diagonal, still active — and after Re8, c4, d4, g4 you're still worse but very much still playing a real game instead of handing over material for free. Always trace the diagonals your queen crosses before landing her on one.

drills.explanation: Your e5 pawn was attacked by the d6 pawn; exd6 resolves it cleanly, and after cxd6 you develop normally with Nc3 and Nf3, dead level. Pushing e6 instead placed the pawn on a square Black's f7 pawn covers: fxe6 ate it for free, and after Bd3 Nf6 c4 you were simply a pawn down out of the opening.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black just pushed ...d6 to challenge your pawn on e5, and pushing e6 instead of capturing doesn't save it — it just delays the loss and hands Black a free developing move, since fxe6 grabs the pawn straight back and you're down the same material but with a worse structure. Capturing with exd6 was simplest and best: after cxd6 the position is balanced pawn-for-pawn, your bishop stays comfortable on f4, and you continue developing naturally with Nc3 and Nf3. When a pawn of yours gets attacked by an enemy pawn, capturing it is almost always cleaner than pushing past and hoping it survives.

drills.explanation: Your queen on e5 was attacked by the knight on f3, and Qe6 was the safe square — it stays active and out of reach, and if Nd4 chases it again, Qe5 returns with White having nothing better than repeating. Qd6 stepped onto the open d-file instead: Rad1 hit the queen with your own rook on d8 lined up behind it, and after Qb4, Rxd8+ Bxd8 handed White the file and the initiative.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (859) — Polish Opening
drills.coachNote: Your queen was beautifully placed on e5, centralized and flexible, and Qd6 gives that up for no reason — it crowds your own rook on d8 and invites Rad1, adding a second attacker down the file that your queen and rook alone can't hold. That pressure forces Qb4, and after Rxd8+ Bxd8 you've been shoved into a trade on White's terms, dropping about three and a half pawns of evaluation even though material stayed level, because your remaining pieces end up passive. Qe6 keeps the same central control without blocking your own rook, so when White's knight hops to d4 attacking the queen, you simply slide back to e5 and the position stays balanced. Keep your queen off squares your own rook needs.
